content: The references provided are a collection of scientific studies, guidelines, and systematic reviews related to various medical topics, including hepatitis, HIV, co-infections, non-communicable diseases, and public health strategies. 1. Peacock et al. (2019) conducted a study estimating the prevalence of hepatitis C infection among individuals who recently injected drugs, providing global, regional, and country-level data. This research was published in the journal Addiction. 2. Trickey et al. (2019) explored the role of injection drug use in the transmission of hepatitis C virus (HCV) on a global, regional, and country-specific scale through a modeling study. The findings were published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) released guidelines on hepatitis B and C testing, emphasizing policy recommendations for effective testing strategies. These guidelines were accessed in June 2021. 4. Easterbrook et al. (2016) provided WHO testing guidance for chronic hepatitis C infection, specifically targeting lowand middle-income countries. This was published in The Journal of Hepatology. 5. Platt et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to determine the prevalence and burden of HCV co-infection in people living with HIV globally. The study was published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 6. Jin et al. (2021) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the prevalence and incidence of HCV infection among men who have sex with men. The findings were published in The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. 7. WHO issued guidelines for the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic hepatitis C infection, focusing on evidence-based approaches. These guidelines were accessed in June 2021. 8. Sikavi et al. (2018) reviewed the management of hepatitis C and HIV co-infection in the era of direct-acting antiviral agents, highlighting improved treatment outcomes. This study appeared in Hepatology. 9. WHO developed guidelines for preventing mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B virus, including recommendations for antiviral prophylaxis during pregnancy. These guidelines were accessed in June 2021. 10. WHO also released comprehensive guidelines for the prevention, care, and treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection, emphasizing public health strategies. These were accessed in June 2021. 11. The WHO website provides detailed information on hepatitis, including its prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. This resource was accessed in June 2021. 12. The WHO Prequalification Programme ensures the quality, safety, and efficacy of medicines, including those for hepatitis and other diseases. This program was accessed in June 2021. 13. WHO published a position paper on hepatitis B vaccines in July 2017, outlining recommendations for their use in public health programs. This document was accessed in June 2021. 14. The HEP Drug Interactions online database provides information on potential drug interactions involving hepatitis treatments. This resource was accessed in June 2021. 15. WHO issued recommendations for screening donated blood to prevent transfusion-transmissible infections, ensuring blood safety. These guidelines were accessed in June 2021. 16. The World Malaria Report 2020 reviewed two decades of global progress and challenges in malaria control. This report was accessed in June 2021. 17. WHO guidelines for malaria prevention and treatment were published to support healthcare providers in managing the disease effectively. These guidelines were accessed in June 2021. 18. Kawuma et al. (2021) investigated the pharmacokinetics of dolutegravir when co-administered with antimalarial drugs, providing insights into drug interactions. This study was published in The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy. 19. WHO released guidance for the treatment of Mycobacterium ulcerans disease (Buruli ulcer), focusing on healthcare worker training. This document was accessed in June 2021. 20. O’Brien et al. (2014) examined the management of Buruli ulcer and HIV co-infection, highlighting the challenges and outcomes. This study was published in Tropical Medicine & International Health. 21. Asiedu et al. edited a comprehensive resource on Buruli ulcer, detailing the epidemiology, diagnosis, and treatment of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection. This publication was accessed in June 2021. 22. Haas et al. (2020) conducted a cohort study in Cape Town, South Africa, to assess excess mortality associated with mental illness in people living with HIV. The findings were published in The Lancet Global Health. 23. Johnson et al. (2008) investigated the association between HIV infection and Mycobacterium ulcerans disease in Benin, providing epidemiological insights. This study was published in AIDS. 24. Christinet et al. (2014) analyzed the impact of HIV on the severity of Buruli ulcer disease in Cameroon, using retrospective data. The study was published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases. 25. Tuffour et al. (2015) described challenges in managing Buruli ulcer and HIV co-infection in a treatment center in Ghana through a case series study. This research was published in The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. 26. Kibadi et al. (2010) reported on Buruli ulcer lesions in HIV-positive patients, emphasizing the clinical implications. This study appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. 27. Johnson et al. (2002) presented a case study of disseminated Mycobacterium ulcerans disease in an HIV-positive patient, highlighting diagnostic and treatment challenges. This study was published in AIDS. 28. Toll et al. (2005) described a case of aggressive multifocal Buruli ulcer with osteomyelitis in an HIV-positive patient, emphasizing the need for multidisciplinary care. This study was published in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology. 29. Bayonne Manou et al. (2013) reviewed cases of Mycobacterium ulcerans disease in Gabon from 2005 to 2011, providing epidemiological data. This study was published in Médecine et Santé Tropicales. 30. Amerson and Maurer (2011) discussed immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome and its impact on tropical dermatoses, including Buruli ulcer. This review was published in Dermatologic Clinics. 31. WHO established a laboratory network and external quality assessment program for PCR-based diagnosis of Buruli ulcer in the African region. This initiative was accessed in June 2021. 32. WHO provided guidance on sampling techniques for laboratory confirmation of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection, supporting accurate diagnosis. This document was accessed in June 2021. 33. WHO released a technical update on managing Buruli ulcer and HIV co-infection, addressing clinical and operational challenges. This update was accessed in June 2021. 34. Davy-Mendez et al. (2020) analyzed hospitalization rates and outcomes among people living with HIV in the southeastern United States from 1996 to 2016. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 35. Burza et al. (2018) reviewed the epidemiology and treatment of leishmaniasis, emphasizing its global burden. This study was published in The Lancet. 36. WHO developed guidelines for treating visceral leishmaniasis in HIV co-infected individuals in East Africa and South-East Asia. These guidelines are forthcoming. 37. Guedes et al. (2021) investigated asymptomatic Leishmania infection in HIV-positive outpatients on antiretroviral therapy in Brazil. This study was published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 38. WHO reported on global leishmaniasis surveillance from 2017 to 2018, introducing new indicators for monitoring progress. This report was accessed in June 2021. 39. Diro et al. (2014) examined visceral leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection in East Africa, highlighting diagnostic and treatment challenges. This study was published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 40. Burza et al. (2014) described the underdiagnosed threat of HIV and visceral leishmaniasis co-infection in Bihar, India, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 41. Monge-Maillo and Lopez-Velez (2016) reviewed treatment options for visceral leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection, providing evidence-based recommendations. This review was published in AIDS Reviews. 42. Sunyoto et al. (2019) explored barriers to the effective supply of leishmaniasis medicines and diagnostics in Eastern Africa through a qualitative study. This research was published in BMJ Open. 43. WHO maintains a Model List of Essential Medicines, ensuring access to critical treatments for various diseases. This resource was accessed in June 2021. 44. Van Griensven et al. (2014) called for concerted action to address visceral leishmaniasis and HIV co-infection, emphasizing the need for integrated care. This study was published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 45. Arbyn et al. (2020) estimated the global incidence and mortality of cervical cancer in 2018, providing a comprehensive analysis. This study was published in The Lancet Global Health. 46. Stelzle et al. (2021) assessed the global burden of cervical cancer associated with HIV, highlighting disparities in disease outcomes. This study was published in The Lancet Global Health. 47. WHO updated its case definitions and clinical staging for HIV-related diseases in adults and children, supporting surveillance and management. This document was accessed in June 2021. 48. Liu et al. (2018) demonstrated that HIV-positive women have a higher risk of HPV infection, precancerous lesions, and cervical cancer. This study was published in AIDS. 49. Massad et al. (2014) examined the long-term detection of HPV among HIV-positive women, providing insights into viral persistence. This study was published in AIDS. 50. Debeaudrap et al. (2019) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on treatment failure for cervical lesions in HIV-infected women. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases. 51. WHO developed a global strategy to eliminate cervical cancer as a public health problem, emphasizing prevention and treatment. This strategy was accessed in June 2021. 52. Canfell et al. (2020) modeled the mortality impact of achieving WHO cervical cancer elimination targets in 78 lowand lower-middle-income countries. This study was published in The Lancet. 53. Brisson et al. (2020) analyzed the impact of HPV vaccination and cervical screening on cervical cancer elimination in 78 lowand lower-middle-income countries. This study was published in The Lancet. 54. Simms et al. (2019) evaluated the potential for global cervical cancer elimination through scaled-up HPV vaccination and screening in 181 countries. This study was published in The Lancet Oncology. 55. Hall et al. (2021) modeled the elimination of cervical cancer in Tanzania, considering the context of endemic HIV infection and active HIV control. This study was published in The International Journal of Cancer. 56. WHO issued guidelines for screening and treating precancerous lesions to prevent cervical cancer, supporting public health efforts. This document was accessed in June 2021. 57. WHO published a position paper on HPV vaccines in May 2017, outlining their role in preventing cervical cancer. This document was accessed in June 2021. 58. WHO developed a package of essential non-communicable disease interventions for primary healthcare, supporting integrated care delivery. This package was accessed in June 2021. 59. WHO released the Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (2013–2020), outlining strategies for reducing disease burden. This plan was accessed in June 2021. 60. Smith et al. (2014) analyzed trends in causes of death among people with HIV from 1999 to 2011, highlighting the impact of antiretroviral therapy. This study was published in The Lancet. 61. Haregu et al. (2012) reviewed the epidemiology of HIV/AIDS and non-communicable disease comorbidity in developing countries, emphasizing the need for integrated care. This study was published in The Journal of Global Healthcare Systems. 62. Crothers et al. (2006) reported an increased prevalence of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease among HIV-positive veterans compared to HIV-negative individuals. This study was published in Chest. 63. Peck et al. (2014) examined the relationship between hypertension, kidney disease, HIV, and antiretroviral therapy among Tanzanian adults. This study was published in BMC Medicine. 64. Johnson et al. (2013) analyzed life expectancies of South African adults starting antiretroviral therapy, using data from cohort studies. This study was published in PLOS Medicine. 65. Crum-Cianflone et al. (2009) investigated trends in cancer incidence among HIV-infected individuals over 20 years, highlighting the impact of antiretroviral therapy. This study was published in AIDS. 66. Reiss (2012) reviewed the interplay between HIV, comorbidity, and aging, emphasizing the challenges of managing older HIV-positive individuals. This study was published in The Journal of the International AIDS Society. 67. Negin et al. (2012) discussed the challenges of aging with HIV in Africa, focusing on the implications of longer life expectancy. This study was published in AIDS. 68. Nigatu (2012) explored the integration of HIV and non-communicable disease care in lowand middle-income countries, highlighting opportunities for health system strengthening. This study was published in Preventing Chronic Disease. 69. Rabkin and Nishtar (2011) proposed leveraging HIV programs to scale up chronic care systems for non-communicable diseases. This study was published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 70. Currier et al. (2003) reviewed the prevalence of coronary heart disease in HIV-infected individuals, emphasizing the role of antiretroviral therapy. This study was published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 71. Islam et al. (2012) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the relative risk of cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV. This study was published in HIV Medicine. 72. Paisible et al. (2015) examined the cardiovascular risk profile and risk of acute myocardial infarction in HIV-infected individuals. This study was published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 73. Chow et al. (2012) compared the incidence of ischemic stroke in HIV-infected and non-HIV-infected patients within a U.S. healthcare system. This study was published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes. 74. Triant et al. (2007) reported increased rates of acute myocardial infarction and cardiovascular risk factors among HIV-positive patients. This study was published in The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism. 75. Marcus et al. (2014) investigated the association between HIV infection and the incidence of ischemic stroke, providing insights into cardiovascular risks. This study was published in AIDS.
